note: The Periodic Table of Speculative Ideas: twelve families and fifteen operators, one hundred and eighty cells.

families.name: COSMOS
families.label: COSMOS
families.note: Cosmic scale tends to hide the fact that a constant produces bodies, infrastructures, and moral limits.

families.name: SPACE
families.label: SPACE AND GEOMETRY
families.note: Modified topology redistributes access before it redistributes wealth: a new adjacency is immediately a new border, escape route, market, and military fact.

families.name: TIME
families.label: TIME AND CAUSALITY
families.note: A serious temporal anomaly immediately produces rights, inheritances, debts, competing testimonies, and incompatible claims about responsibility.

families.name: LIFE
families.label: LIFE AND EVOLUTION
families.note: Alternative biology becomes fertile when it changes ecology, kinship, labor, and politics rather than merely changing skin.

families.name: MIND
families.label: MIND AND IDENTITY
families.note: Functional similarity does not by itself settle consciousness, rights, continuity, or the number of persons present.

families.name: BODY
families.label: BODY AND METAMORPHOSIS
families.note: The body becomes political infrastructure when it can be replaced, designed, copied, distributed, or externalized.

families.name: INFORMATION
families.label: INFORMATION AND LANGUAGE
families.note: More information can move scarcity toward relevance, privacy, provenance, trust, and the ability to remain unmodeled.

families.name: SOCIETY
families.label: SOCIETY AND POWER
families.note: Institutions do not disappear when technology solves one scarcity; they reorganize around new scarcities, vetoes, dependencies, and prestige.

families.name: ARTIFACT
families.label: MACHINES AND ARTIFACTS
families.note: A machine’s original purpose does not remain legitimate merely because it is old; once it enters history, it acquires ecology, politics, and successors.

families.name: CONTACT
families.label: CONTACT AND CIVILIZATIONS
families.note: Successful contact may sometimes consist in preserving a stable limit of interpretation rather than forcing the other into familiar categories.

families.name: FANTASY
families.label: FANTASY AND MAGICAL ONTOLOGIES
families.note: Magic becomes analytically interesting when cost, access, exception, oath, and refusal become institutions rather than decoration.

families.name: META-REALITY
families.label: SCIENCE FANTASY AND META-REALITY
families.note: Reflexivity is the region where the classifier must be included in its own classification and where descriptions can become causes.

operators.name: ALTERATION
operators.does: changes the value or form of an existing rule without yet changing the kind of thing on which it operates

operators.name: SUBSTITUTION
operators.does: replaces the substrate, carrier, or medium of a function

operators.name: EXTENSION
operators.does: adds a degree of freedom, capacity, or axis absent from the baseline world

operators.name: RATE
operators.does: changes the speed at which processes unfold without necessarily changing their order

operators.name: BOUNDARY
operators.does: moves, perforates, or redefines the boundary between inside and outside

operators.name: DISTRIBUTION
operators.does: spreads a unit across several bodies, places, agents, or nodes

operators.name: COPYING
operators.does: creates a second instance similar enough for continuity to become a problem

operators.name: COUPLING
operators.does: makes previously independent domains determine one another

operators.name: EXTERNALIZATION
operators.does: turns an internal property into an object, companion, infrastructure, or institution

operators.name: INVERSION
operators.does: reverses an order, dependence, direction, or relation taken as natural

operators.name: LOOP
operators.does: feeds a system output back into its own input, producing recurrence

operators.name: GENESIS
operators.does: allows a system to create new agents, worlds, laws, or substrates

operators.name: SCARCITY SHIFT
operators.does: makes what was rare abundant, or what was abundant rare, forcing a new economy of power

operators.name: REFLEXIVITY
operators.does: makes description, prediction, belief, or observation modify the thing described

operators.name: OUTFINITE
operators.does: allows successive finite extensions without postulating an already-given final infinite state

elements.name: Alternative Gravity

sections.Nucleus: Negotiated Unknown enters the Atlas as a mutation distinct enough that, if removed from a well-built world, major consequences would have to be rewritten. In its minimal form, the idea says that a world has the right to remain partly misunderstood. Its family is science fantasy and meta-reality, and the control question is: what happens when the rule is no longer background but an object of design?
sections.Genealogy: A useful literary landmark is final thesis. The reference does not claim an absolute “first invention.” Science fiction and fantasy function as megatexts: motifs migrate, combine, and reappear. In the Table, the work is treated as a memorable isotope of the idea: a particular realization showing what the element can do when propagated beyond the premise.
sections.Periodic position: The element is associated with the outfinite operator: allows successive finite extensions without postulating an already-given final infinite state. The corresponding abstract symbol is RO. This double representation separates mechanism from historical example. An author may combine several elements, and the same concrete idea may have secondary links to other families; the Table does not demand purity, only makes the bonds visible.
sections.Propagation: A serious implementation must show who gains new access, who loses an old protection, and which everyday metaphors stop working. Reflexivity is the region where the classifier must be included in its own classification and where descriptions can become causes. In this sense, social consequence is part of the operational definition of the element, not a sociological appendix.
sections.Instability: The element becomes narratively fertile when it solves one problem and creates another. A world in which a world has the right to remain partly misunderstood should not automatically be better or worse; it should have different failure boundaries. The question “who can say no?” works here as a political test, and “what can we no longer distinguish?” as an epistemic test.
sections.Compounds: In Kesh’s laboratory, Un is used alone only for demonstrations. Combined with a time element it can produce new forms of responsibility; with a mind element it can change the person; with a social element it can produce unexpected institutions; with reflexivity it can make the world react to its own description. Choose one and propagate it. Alternative gravity must reach the skeleton, architecture, sport, war, religion, and language. Uploading must reach inheritance, punishment, marriage, insurance, and mourning. Contract magic must reach the legal profession, the education of children, and the way a society defines consent. Only after propagation do you add a second element. The combination must produce interference. Post-scarcity plus reputation does not mean two independent features; free goods move competition toward status, and reputation can become a new infrastructure of exclusion. Branching time plus a mental copy does not merely mean two kinds of multiplication; together they create persons who may share the same past in different branches and raise questions about debts between versions. The third step is to change the observer. A world is not finished while every important question is still being asked by a contemporary human with better technology. A Tine, an ocean like Solaris, a Culture Mind, a heptapod, or a being living in neutron matter should not be anthropomorphic scenery. Ask which human distinction becomes provincial from its point of view. The fourth step is the refusal test. Who can refuse the technology, the god, the contract, the algorithm, or the intervention? What price do they pay? If the only answer is that refusal is irrational, the world 673 has already absorbed the author’s ideology into its laws of nature and deserves closer examination. The fifth step is the exteriority test. Do not explain everything. Gratuitous mystery is laziness, but total explanation can also destroy the object it claims to respect. A sufficiently alien civilization may leave zones of stable incomprehension; a social system may contain tensions that do not reduce to a single cause; a person may have a right to private processes even against their creator. The final step is periodic revision. Ask whether the idea you built fits an existing cell. If it does not, do not force it. It may be an unusual compound, a new isotope, or a demand for a new family. Aster finds neither a technology that can restore her innocence nor a world exotic enough to remain surprising forever. Every surprise she understands becomes memory; every memory can become a model. The problem was never too few universes. The change is political and almost modest. Aster accepts limits she is not physically compelled to accept. She does not inspect the children’s private processes. She does not follow Tern across the threshold. She does not treat opacity as a defect to be repaired. She does not turn her Hunger into a debt owed by those she loves. The Table remains. In this edition it has one hundred and eighty cells, hundreds of isotopes, a chemistry of compounds, and one institutionally empty cell. It does not claim to be the final catalog of imagination. Such a claim would contradict the very lesson that made it possible. On a very late night, a pattern appears at the edge of Aster’s instruments. It might be Tern, noise, a new civilization, or an echo of her own systems. She has enough power to increase resolution until the mystery yields, if the mystery belongs to her domain. She does not. For the first time in a very long while, the unknown does not feel like a wound asking to be healed. It feels like a form of neighborhood. 676
